title: Etiquette in Asymmetric Power Relations
paragraphs: Traditional etiquette frameworks, developed predominantly for interactions among relative social equals, prove inadequately calibrated for the genuinely asymmetric power relationships increasingly characterizing contemporary professional and institutional contexts, where conventional courtesy norms may inadvertently obscure rather than address underlying power imbalance.

This inadequacy manifests particularly regarding feedback and disagreement, wherein etiquette conventions emphasizing deference toward hierarchical superiors can effectively suppress legitimate concerns that subordinates possess compelling substantive reason to raise but hesitate voicing given etiquette's implicit hierarchical deference expectations.

Some organizations have attempted addressing this tension through explicit norms encouraging upward feedback regardless of hierarchical position, though implementing such norms proves genuinely difficult given how deeply conventional deference etiquette remains embedded within organizational culture despite formal policy encouraging different behavior.

This difficulty suggests that meaningfully addressing power asymmetry's effect on communication requires more than formal policy alone, potentially requiring hierarchical superiors to actively model receptiveness toward upward challenge in ways that substantively counter conventional deference expectations rather than merely declaring such challenge formally welcome.

Even successful cultural change toward more genuine upward communication likely requires sustained, consistent effort given how deeply conventional hierarchical etiquette remains embedded within broader social conditioning extending well beyond any single organizational context.

This persistent challenge suggests that appropriately calibrating etiquette for genuinely asymmetric power relationships remains an evolving practical and theoretical problem, requiring continued attention as organizations increasingly recognize conventional deference norms' potential costs to substantive communication and organizational effectiveness.
